title: Team Members Who Consistently Misinterpret Your Directions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece addresses the frustrating pattern of team members who seem to hear something entirely different from what a leader intended, not out of defiance, but because self-focus distorts how they interpret instructions. The author's proposed fix isn't clearer explanation, it's more specific, action-oriented phrasing. Instructions that describe what NOT to do are easy to misread; instructions that specify a concrete action to take are much harder to misinterpret. The piece uses the example of asking someone to stand down on an issue, reframing it instead as asking them to gather more data, to illustrate the shift from passive to active instruction.
points: Some team members consistently misinterpret directions, often unintentionally, hearing what they want to hear
Explaining instructions more thoroughly or forcefully isn't the fix; specificity is
Instructions describing what NOT to do are far easier to misread than instructions describing a concrete action
Reframing a stand-down request as a specific task (like gathering more data) reduces misinterpretation
quotes: It may be that some team members are simply resistant to directions. Others may deliberately thumb their nose at the leader and chart their own path.
People who consistently misinterpret directions, instructions, and other messages simply hear what they want to hear.
Instead of explaining what they want to see in the future, they get more specific. They ask for specific actions.
This request, like so many other directions that get ignored or misinterpreted, suggests inaction or what the other party should NOT do.
Asking people to act is a much harder message to misinterpret than a request not to act.
